metadata.title: RAG, Explained
metadata.audience: Anyone building with an LLM over their own data

beats.narration_text: How can an AI answer questions about documents it was never trained on? The pattern is called RAG. The model doesn't memorize your files, it looks them up when you ask.

props.command: How does an AI answer from documents it was never trained on?
output: It looks them up at question time.
Retrieve the relevant passages, then answer using them.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Asavari, a fellow at Humanitarians AI. This video explains RAG, retrieval-augmented generation, the pattern that lets an AI answer questions about documents it was never trained on. You'll learn how it works and, more importantly, where it quietly goes wrong. If you're building anything with an LLM over your own data, start here.

props.command: What is this video about, and why should I watch it?
output: Who: Asavari, a Humanitarians AI fellow
Why watch: catch the mistake before it costs you

beats.narration_text: A model only knows what it saw during training. Ask about your internal document, last week's filing, anything private, and it either admits it doesn't know or, far more often, invents something that sounds right. That confident invention is the hallucination. The model isn't lying, it just has no source.

props.artifactTitle: A model only knows what it was trained on
artifactLines: Ask about a private or recent document
It's not in the training data
The model invents something that sounds right — the hallucination

beats.narration_text: Your documents are split into chunks and indexed so they can be searched by meaning. When a question comes in, the system finds the passages most relevant to it, hands them to the model, and says, answer using this. So the answer is grounded in retrieved text, with citations you can check.

props.artifactTitle: Retrieve the right passages, then generate
artifactLines: Documents split into chunks, indexed by meaning
Question -> find the most relevant passages
Passages handed to the model: 'answer using this' -> answer + citations

beats.narration_text: The catch people skip. RAG doesn't fix hallucination, it moves the risk. If retrieval pulls the wrong passages, the model writes a fluent, confident answer on the wrong evidence, and it looks just as trustworthy. So the hard problem is retrieval, chunking, search quality, and knowing when nothing relevant was found.

props.artifactTitle: RAG is only as good as what it retrieves
artifactLines: Retrieve the wrong passages -> a fluent answer on the wrong evidence
It looks just as trustworthy as a correct one
The hard problem isn't generation — it's retrieval
props.sparkLine: Garbage retrieval in, confident garbage out.

beats.narration_text: Judge a RAG system not by how good the answer sounds. Ask whether it cites the passages it used, and whether you can open them. Ask what it does when nothing relevant exists. And ask whether anyone measures retrieval quality. An answer you can trace beats a polished one you can't. No source, no verdict.

props.artifactTitle: Judge a RAG system by its retrieval, not its prose
props.artifactHeading: Citations you can open beat prose you can't
artifactLines: Does the answer cite the passages it used?
Can you open those sources and verify?
What happens when nothing relevant is found?
Is retrieval measured — or just the vibe?
